opus-5.5.text:
I think about it as a spectrum of abstraction levels, and each tool picks a different point on that spectrum with different tradeoffs.

Triton, I'd say, has been incredibly successful because it hit a sweet spot. It lets you write kernels at the level of blocks or tiles rather than individual threads. You think in terms of "I'm loading this tile of a matrix, doing a matmul on it, writing it out," and the compiler handles a lot of the painful stuff: memory coalescing, shared memory management, some of the scheduling. For a lot of people, especially researchers who know Python and PyTorch, that's a huge productivity win. You can get to maybe 70, 80, sometimes 90 percent of peak performance with a fraction of the effort it would take in raw CUDA. That's why you see so many kernels in the ecosystem written in Triton now.

The tradeoff is that when you need that last bit of performance, especially on the newest hardware, the abstraction can get in your way. On something like Hopper or Blackwell, there are new features like the tensor memory accelerator, warp specialization, asynchronous pipelines, and to really exploit them you sometimes need fine-grained control the compiler doesn't expose, or doesn't expose yet. So for something like FlashAttention, where we're trying to squeeze out every bit, we've often ended up going lower level, with CUDA and CUTLASS, or more recently tools like CuTe DSL that give you Python ergonomics but much more explicit control over layouts and data movement.

Mojo is a somewhat different bet. It's trying to be a general-purpose systems language with Python-like syntax, where you get low-level control, compile-time metaprogramming, and the ability to target different hardware, not just NVIDIA. I think the vision is really interesting, especially the portability angle. The question for any new language is ecosystem and adoption: are people going to write their kernels there, are the compilers mature enough on the latest hardware, does it integrate cleanly with PyTorch and the existing stack. Those things take time.

My general view is there's no single right abstraction. What I'd love to see, and I think the field is converging on, is a layered approach: high-level tools like Triton for the 90 percent of cases where productivity matters most, and lower-level but still ergonomic tools for experts who need full control on the newest hardware. And ideally those layers interoperate, so you can start high-level and drop down only where you need to.

The other thing I'd say is that hardware is moving so fast that whatever abstraction you pick has to keep up. Every new GPU generation changes what the optimal kernel looks like. So the abstractions that win will probably be the ones that can adapt quickly to new hardware features, rather than the ones that look the most elegant on paper today.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because the question underneath it is really: what's the right level of abstraction for writing fast kernels, and who is the audience?

Triton I know very well. The core idea is that you program at the level of a block, or a tile. Instead of thinking about individual threads and warps and which thread loads which element, you say, here's a tile of the matrix, load it, multiply it, store it. And the compiler figures out the thread mapping, the shared memory layout, a lot of the software pipelining. For a huge class of kernels, elementwise ops, reductions, fused attention variants, normalization, that's exactly the right abstraction. You can write something in an afternoon that gets you to maybe 70, 80 percent of what a hand-tuned CUDA kernel does. And honestly, for most researchers, that's the trade you want. Your time is the scarce resource, not the last 20 percent.

Where it gets harder is when you're chasing peak on the newest hardware. Hopper and Blackwell have things like TMA, warp specialization, asynchronous tensor core instructions, and getting those right really requires controlling what each warp group is doing and when. Triton has been adding ways to express that, but there's an inherent tension: the more control you expose, the more you erode the simplicity that was the whole point. That's part of why we ended up writing FlashAttention 3 closer to the metal with CUTLASS and CuTe, because we needed to orchestrate producer and consumer warps explicitly. So I'd say Triton is a great default, and then you drop down when you have evidence you need to.

Mojo I've followed less closely in practice, but the ambition is interesting. They're trying to do something broader. It's not just a kernel DSL, it's a full language with a Python-compatible feel, with compile-time metaprogramming and the ability to go from very high level down to very low level in the same language. The appeal is you don't have this cliff where you leave Python, go into CUDA, and now you're in a totally different world with a different build system and different debugging. If they pull it off, that's a real win for ergonomics. And building on MLIR gives them a serious compiler foundation.

The honest caveat is that the hard part of this space isn't the language design, it's the ecosystem and the hardware-specific knowledge baked in. Triton's advantage is that it's open, it's inside PyTorch, so torch.compile emits Triton, and thousands of people are hitting it and filing bugs and contributing backends. Mojo has been more of a closed, company-driven effort for a while, though that's been changing. For a hardware-dependent tool, how quickly it tracks new GPU features and how many people are writing kernels in it matters as much as how elegant the abstraction is.

So if I had to sum it up: Triton has found a sweet spot that's proven itself, and its main challenge is extending to the newest hardware features without losing what makes it nice. Mojo is a bigger bet on unifying the stack, and the question is whether it gets enough adoption and enough hardware coverage to pay off. I'd love for both to succeed, because right now the alternative is that only a few hundred people in the world can write a kernel that actually saturates an H100 or a B200, and that's a bottleneck for the whole field.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much control the abstraction gives you, and how much complexity it hides. Triton hits a pretty useful point there. You work with blocks of elements rather than writing the behavior of each individual thread, and that makes a lot of GPU kernels much easier to express. You can try an idea, benchmark it, and iterate quickly.

But the hardware details still matter. For something like attention, you care about how data moves between global memory, shared memory, and registers, and how you overlap that movement with computation. If the abstraction doesn’t let you control something you need, getting that last bit of performance can become difficult. So I want a productive default, with a way to go deeper when necessary.

Mojo is interesting in that context, although I’m less familiar with its GPU programming model, so I wouldn’t make a strong performance comparison. The thing I’d look for is whether it makes common kernels straightforward while still letting you express the specialized scheduling and memory operations that demanding kernels need. That’s a difficult balance, and I don’t think there’s one abstraction that’s ideal for every workload.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what you want the abstraction to hide. Triton is a really nice sweet spot: you work with blocks of data, and the compiler handles a lot of the details of mapping those operations onto GPU threads. That makes it much easier to write a fast kernel than starting from CUDA. But when you’re trying to squeeze out the last bit of performance, you may want control over things like data movement, layouts, and how work is divided among warps. Then the abstraction can become a constraint.

Mojo is interesting because it’s aiming for a broader programming model, with high-level ergonomics and access to lower-level control. I’m less familiar with it, so I’d be cautious about making a direct performance comparison.

What I’d like from either approach is a good default that lets you go deeper when you need to. Can I write something simple, see where the bottleneck is, and take control of just that part? That’s a really useful property for GPU programming.
